Note::begin¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note::const_iterator Note::begin() const

Enter The Flat Text Range¶

begin() returns a forward iterator positioned at the first Text or Bytes cell. It is the entry point used by range-based for, standard algorithms, and explicit iterator loops. Iteration is read-only: dereferencing produces a std::string_view, never a mutable string and never a Note slice.

The range is deliberately flat. Rank controls how cells are addressed, not how a C++ iterator nests. A matrix or rank-three Note is visited in row-major logical order, exactly the same order used by at(linear), flatten(), copy_flat_to(), and for_each_flat().

begin() supports Text and Bytes because its value type is std::string_view. For Bool, Int64, and Float64 Notes, traverse the native spans returned by bools(), integers(), and reals(); attempting to call begin() on those dtypes throws before an iterator is returned.

Ownership And Validity¶

The iterator stores an intrusive reference to the Note’s backing arena. The iterator therefore keeps the storage alive even if the original Note handle is destroyed. A std::string_view obtained by dereferencing is still a borrowed view: keep either the iterator or a Note sharing that arena alive while using the view. Construct std::string(*it) when independent ownership is required.

Incrementing a past-the-end iterator or dereferencing end() is invalid. Comparisons are meaningful only for iterators into the same backing Note.

Example 1: Range-Based Iteration¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"north", "east", "south", "west"});
std::cout << '[';
std::size_t index = 0;
for (const std::string_view word : words)
  std::cout << (index++ ? ", " : "") << '"' << word << '"';
std::cout << "] count=" << std::distance(words.begin(), words.end()) << '\n';

Output¶

["north", "east", "south", "west"] count=4

Example 2: Higher Ranks Flatten Row-Major¶

const auto grid = pluss::note::make(
    std::vector<std::string>{"r0c0", "r0c1", "r0c2", "r1c0", "r1c1", "r1c2"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 3});

for (const auto cell : grid) std::cout << cell << ' ';
std::cout << '\n';

Output¶

r0c0 r0c1 r0c2 r1c0 r1c1 r1c2

The iterator does not emit row objects. Use matrix() when each row must remain a Note.

Example 3: Scalar And Empty Ranges¶

const auto scalar = pluss::note::make("solo");
const auto empty = pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::string>{});
std::cout << "scalar distance=" << std::distance(scalar.begin(), scalar.end())
          << " value=" << *scalar.begin() << '\n'
          << "empty distance=" << std::distance(empty.begin(), empty.end())
          << " equal=" << std::boolalpha << (empty.begin() == empty.end()) << '\n';

Output¶

scalar distance=1 value=solo
empty distance=0 equal=true

Example 4: An Iterator Keeps Its Arena Alive¶

auto kept = [] {
  const auto temporary = pluss::note::make({"kept", "alive"});
  return temporary.begin();
}();
std::cout << *kept << ' ';
++kept;
std::cout << *kept << '\n';

Output¶

kept alive

Example 5: Native Dtypes Use Native Spans¶

const auto values = pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{3, 1, 4});
try { (void)values.begin(); }
catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "Int64 begin: rejected\n"; }
std::cout << "integers=";
for (const auto value : values.integers()) std::cout << value << ' ';
std::cout << '\n';

Output¶

Int64 begin: rejected
integers=3 1 4
